subject: pluto-dwarf-planet
title: Why Pluto Is a Dwarf Planet
summary: Pluto did not change in 2006. The rules for what counts as a planet did.

keys.prompt: What are the three rules a planet must pass?
keys.answer: It goes around the Sun, it is round, and it has cleared its path of other big things.

options.text: Goes around the Sun, is round, and has cleared its path
Is big, is hot, and has a moon
Goes around the Sun, has rings, and has air

keys.prompt: Which rule does Pluto not pass?
keys.answer: Pluto has not cleared its path. Lots of other icy objects share its part of space.

options.text: It has not cleared its path of other objects
It does not go around the Sun

keys.prompt: Why did Pluto get a new name for its group in 2006?
keys.answer: Astronomers found other icy worlds like Pluto far out in space, so they made clear rules for what a planet is.

options.text: Scientists found many icy worlds like Pluto and made clear rules
Pluto shrank and got much smaller
Pluto moved closer to the Sun

cards.title: Nine, then eight
cards.text: Your grandparents learned there were nine planets. You learn there are eight. Pluto is still out there, the same as ever. So what changed?

cards.question: Pluto was found in 1930. Who do you think picked its name?
cards.reveal: An 11-year-old girl in England named Venetia Burney picked the name Pluto.

cards.title: Named by a kid
cards.text: Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930. In England, an 11-year-old girl named Venetia Burney heard the news at breakfast. She said it should be named Pluto, after the Roman god of the underworld. Her grandpa passed the idea on, and it was picked.
cards.example: For 76 years after that, Pluto was called the ninth planet.

cards.title: Small and far away
cards.text: Pluto is tiny. It is only about half as wide as the United States. It is so far away that sunlight takes 5.5 hours to get there. It is very, very cold there.
cards.example: Even at noon on Pluto, the light is only as bright as it gets here just around sunset.

cards.title: Three rules for a planet
cards.text: In 2006, a big group of astronomers called the IAU wrote rules for planets. A planet must go around the Sun. It must be big enough that its own gravity pulls it round. And it must have cleared its path of other big objects.
cards.example: Earth passes all three tests. So do the other seven planets.

why.q: Why did astronomers need rules at all?
why.a: They kept finding icy worlds like Pluto far out in space. Without rules, nobody could say which ones were planets.

cards.title: Pluto shares its road
cards.text: Pluto goes around the Sun, and it is round. But it lives in the Kuiper Belt, a zone full of icy objects. Other objects may cross its path. So Pluto fails the third rule. It is now called a dwarf planet.
cards.example: Think of a busy hallway at school. A planet is like a kid who has the whole hallway to themselves. Pluto shares it with a crowd.

cards.title: Still an amazing world
cards.text: In 2015, a spacecraft called New Horizons flew past Pluto. It found mountains made of ice and wide plains of frozen gas. Pluto has five moons too. There are five known dwarf planets, and there may be many more.
cards.example: The five are Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake and Eris.

cards.question: Do you think Pluto should be a planet? If you could write the rules, what would yours be?
nudges: Would your rules let in lots of new planets, or just a few?
Is it fair to change a name after people learned it?

sources.title: Pluto: Facts
sources.supports: Pluto discovered in 1930; named by 11-year-old Venetia Burney of England, who suggested it at breakfast after the Roman god of the underworld, and her grandfather forwarded it; about half the width of the United States; sunlight takes 5.5 hours to reach it; midday light on Pluto matches the brightness near sunset on Earth; reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 by the IAU; other objects might cross its orbit in the Kuiper Belt; mountains of water ice and plains of frozen nitrogen; five moons; New Horizons flew by in 2015.

sources.title: Dwarf Planets
sources.supports: The IAU's 2006 planet rules: orbit the Sun, be mostly round, and clear away other objects near its orbit; dwarf planets have not cleared their orbits; five recognized dwarf planets (Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, Eris) and maybe more than a hundred more; Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto in 1930; other worlds found in the Kuiper Belt led to the change.
